newsitem.title: UK: EUROPEAN PETROL MARGINS HIT BY STRONG DOLLAR.
newsitem.headline: EUROPEAN PETROL MARGINS HIT BY STRONG DOLLAR.

text.p: Petrol retail margins in continental Europe have been hit by the recent dramatic rise in the dollar, the currency of spot oil trade, coinciding with a recent jump in wholesale gasoline prices, analysts said on Tuesday.
But while local gasoline prices have gone into reverse in recent days, the dollar remains extremely strong against leading continental European currencies.

The dollar's strength meant that from January 10 to August 6, when wholesale gasoline barge prices rose by $55 a tonne or by 30 percent, German prices rose by 37 percent and Belgian prices by 41 percent.

The currency shift has been seen placing severe pressure on retailing margins in already fiercely competitive markets characterised by the price-cutting influence of hypermakets and other specialist retailers.
Exxon Corp's Esso Germany spokesman Karl Schult-Bornemann said the appreciating dollar coupled with requirements this year for environmental investments at petrol forecourts were margin "headaches."
But he said sector fundamentals in Germany were reasonable, given long-established competitive structures associated with the ease of imports from the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) oil trade hub.
"The highest petrol prices in Germany are equivalent to Rotterdam gasoline cargo prices plus transport," he said.

Andrew Bradley of Edinburgh-based industry analysts Wood Mackenzie expected medium to long term margins to weaken in Germany, given higher costs of environmental improvements and no change in hypermarkets' policy of using petrol as their loss leader.
In France, meanwhile, he saw no prospect that "margins will ever climb appreciably" given the strong position of the hypermarkets, who control around 50 percent of the French petrol retail market.

But the short term is likely to see some easing of pressures given an expected seasonal decline in wholesale gasoline prices as the end of the summer driving season approaches, said Peter Regnier of British-based analysts Oil Price Assessments Ltd (OPAL).
A $25 reversal in prompt prices on the ARA barge market since last Friday is already leading to a partial reversal of petrol pump price hikes in countries that saw strong gains only last week.

Regnier said Belgian suppliers were set on Wednesday to cut the price of premium unleaded by 0.90 francs a litre, having raised the price by 2.0 francs in three successive moves between July 29 and August 8.
He said German prices were likely to end this week below last Friday's levels despite a possible hike over the next day or two.
Italian oil companies were forced by political pressure to cut their pump prices by 10 lire a litre this week after abandoning calls for a five lire rise last week.
The dollar rose from DM1.54 at the start of this year to hit a DM1.88 peak last week before slipping to 1.86 Tuesday.
Against the Belgian franc, the dollar stood at 38.50 francs on Tuesday, up from 32 on January 1, and to 6.3 French francs from 5.2 francs on January 1.
